rationale: The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few large blink, movement or muscle bursts can dominate the mean-averaged Welch spectrum and blur the delta/theta increase and alpha decrease seen in schizophrenia. This change averages the Welch segments with the median instead of the mean. That is a simple, parameter-free form of artifact rejection, and it should also make the features more stable on the short 1-minute external recordings.

Schizophrenia has been linked to a changed aperiodic (1/f) exponent of the EEG spectrum, which reflects excitation/inhibition balance (Molina et al. 2020). This change adds a per-channel aperiodic slope: a least-squares fit of log-power against log-frequency over 2–40 Hz, with the alpha-peak region (7–14 Hz) excluded. The fit uses the same median Welch PSD as the current features. Only the slope is used, not the offset, so the new features don't depend on amplitude scale and should carry over to the external amplifiers.

The recordings keep their original reference, and the external datasets (MSU, RepOD) use different references and amplifiers. A reference electrode that picks up its own alpha or muscle activity spreads that activity into every channel's relative band power, so the features partly describe the reference rather than the patient. This change re-references each recording to the common average of the 16 channels before the median-Welch PSD, which should give reference-independent topographies of the schizophrenia delta/theta increase and alpha decrease that transfer better across clinics.

This change adds each channel's individual alpha frequency, measured as the centre of gravity of the 7–13 Hz median-Welch PSD on 4 s segments for finer frequency resolution. Slower alpha is a well-replicated finding in schizophrenia, and fixed 8–13 Hz bands only partly capture that shift. The measure is in Hz, so it doesn't depend on amplitude scale, reference gain or recording length, which should help it carry over to the external datasets.

Higuchi fractal dimension is one of the most consistently reported EEG markers of schizophrenia (changed signal complexity), and spectral power alone does not capture it. This change adds one Higuchi FD value per channel, computed on 1–45 Hz band-passed 4 s epochs and median-aggregated across epochs. The median keeps artifacts out, the measure doesn't change with amplitude scale, and it is stable across recording lengths, which should help on the external datasets.

Schizophrenia is often described as a disorder of disconnection, and so far the model has no connectivity features. This change adds each channel's mean weighted phase-lag index (wPLI) to all other channels in the delta, theta, alpha and beta bands. It uses 1–45 Hz filtered 2 s epochs and drops epochs with extreme amplitude first. wPLI ignores zero-lag coupling, so volume conduction and the shared reference have little effect on it. It also doesn't depend on amplitude scale, which should help it carry over to the external amplifiers.

This adds per-channel permutation entropy (order 4) at two time scales, delay 1 (fast, beta/gamma) and delay 3 (slower, theta/alpha). Each is computed on 1–45 Hz filtered 4 s epochs and median-aggregated across epochs. Schizophrenia is repeatedly reported to change the irregularity of the EEG signal, and ordinal-pattern entropy measures this in a different way from the spectrum or Higuchi FD. It is also unaffected by amplitude scale or gain, and robust to recording length, which should help on the external amplifiers.

I'm adding EEG microstate features. Microstate class C/D changes are among the most replicated EEG findings in schizophrenia (Rieger et al. 2016 meta-analysis), and the current features don't capture these fast topographic dynamics. The method computes 2–20 Hz average-referenced maps at peaks of global field power, with artifact peaks dropped. It clusters them into 4 polarity-invariant templates with a label-free modified k-means across all subjects, then orders the templates against canonical A/B/C/D shapes built from electrode positions, so class labels stay consistent on the external sets. Each subject's recording is then fitted back to the templates to get per-class coverage, log mean duration, occurrence rate, and the share of signal variance the templates explain. None of these features depend on amplitude scale, reference or recording length.

I'm adding microstate transition probabilities: for each of the 4 classes, the probability of switching to each of the other 3 classes, 12 values per subject in total. Schizophrenia is reported to change the order in which microstates follow each other, not just how often each occurs (Lehmann et al. 2005; Tomescu et al.), and the current coverage/duration/occurrence features don't capture that order. These values come from the same template fit the model already uses, and they don't depend on amplitude scale, reference or recording length.

Rescale each standardized feature family so it contributes equally to the logistic L2 penalty. The families are relative power (80 features per condition), Higuchi FD (16), permutation entropy (32), wPLI (64) and microstates (13). Right now the 80 relative-power features take most of the weight in the penalty, while the small microstate and complexity blocks, which gave the biggest gains, are relatively over-penalized. Equal weighting should let these independent schizophrenia markers count evenly and make the model less reliant on any one family, which may matter on the external clinics. Each weight is `sqrt(D/(n_blocks·d_b))`, so the total feature norm and the effective meaning of C=0.1 stay about the same. If the feature layout is not what the code expects, it falls back to equal per-feature weights.

The model's only connectivity measure is wPLI, which captures phase coupling. Schizophrenia is also reported to change amplitude-envelope coupling (slow co-fluctuation of band power between regions, Hipp et al. 2012), and that is a separate network property. This change adds each channel's leakage-corrected (orthogonalized) amplitude-envelope correlation (AEC) node strength in the theta, alpha and beta bands. Orthogonalization removes zero-lag coupling (volume conduction and the shared reference), and the log of 0.25 s binned envelopes makes the measure independent of amplitude scale and resistant to large artifact bursts.

This adds per-channel Lempel-Ziv complexity: each 1–45 Hz filtered 4 s epoch is converted to 0/1 by comparing it to its own median, then scored, and the median over epochs is kept. Reduced LZ complexity is a repeatedly reported marker in schizophrenia (Li et al. 2008; Fernández et al. 2011). It measures how many distinct patterns the signal produces over time, which Higuchi FD (geometric roughness) and permutation entropy (short ordinal motifs) don't capture. Because each epoch is split at its own median, the measure doesn't depend on amplitude scale or gain, and the median over epochs keeps it stable across recording lengths.

Instead of hard-coding the L2 strength at C=0.1, choose it by inner grouped CV on the training fold: three repeats of 5-fold CV over subject groups, scored by AUROC, on a log grid of C values. Ties go to the stronger penalty. Since round 1 the feature set has grown from about 80 to about 205 dimensions while there are only about 80 training subjects, so the C that was fixed for the small feature set is unlikely to still be right. The extra repeats reduce the selection noise that comes with small n.

This adds a second model built on spatial covariance in Riemannian tangent space and averages its probability with the current logistic model. The covariance comes from three bands (1–8, 8–13 and 13–30 Hz), with the same artifact-epoch rejection, average reference, trace normalization and shrinkage. Covariance captures how strongly channels co-vary in amplitude at zero lag, and none of the current features do: wPLI ignores zero-lag coupling, relative power is per channel, and microstates are discrete. Fitting it as a separate model rather than adding its 408 features to the existing ones avoids crowding out the compact blocks that gave the earlier gains. Average reference plus trace normalization should keep the new features independent of the reference and amplitude scale used by external amplifiers. I haven't run this, so I don't know the Dev score yet.

I'm splitting the slow covariance band (1–8 Hz) in the Riemannian model into delta (1–4 Hz) and theta (4–8 Hz). Schizophrenia's delta increase (widespread, possibly subcortical in origin) and its frontal-midline theta increase come from different spatial generators, and pooling them into one covariance matrix blurs both topographies. Not run yet, so I don't have a Dev score.

The Riemannian model learns from only about 80 subject-level covariance matrices. I'm now computing each subject's band covariances on 4 contiguous chunks of clean epochs, so each subject gives 4 matrices. The tangent-space model is fitted on all of them, with C divided by 4 so the penalty per subject stays the same, and the 4 test-chunk probabilities are averaged. This is a hypothesis: it should add realistic within-subject variability for the small-n model, act as test-time averaging over parts of the recording, and match the short 1-minute external recordings better than a single 5-minute average does. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score yet.

I'm adding per-channel multiscale sample entropy (m=2, r=0.2·SD of each epoch, at coarse-graining scales 1 and 4) to the main logistic model. It is computed on 1–45 Hz filtered 8 s epochs, up to 20 evenly spaced epochs per channel, and median-aggregated. Schizophrenia shows scale-dependent changes in EEG regularity (Takahashi et al. 2010). Sample entropy measures how well amplitude patterns repeat, which permutation entropy (ordinal order only), Higuchi FD (geometric roughness) and LZC (which didn't help) don't capture. The tolerance is set relative to each epoch's SD, so the features don't depend on amplitude scale, and the median over epochs keeps them stable on 1-minute recordings. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score yet.

Nikulin et al. (2012) reported weaker long-range temporal correlations in the alpha and beta amplitude envelopes in schizophrenia. This change adds that measure as one detrended-fluctuation-analysis (DFA) exponent per channel for the alpha (8–13 Hz) and beta (13–30 Hz) amplitude envelopes, added to the main logistic model. None of the current features capture how oscillation amplitude persists over seconds; all of them are static or very fast. The exponent is a log-log slope fitted over fixed 1–10 s windows, so it doesn't depend on amplitude scale or reference gain and can still be estimated on the 1-minute external recordings. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score yet.

I'm adding per-channel Hjorth mobility and complexity (log-scaled), computed on the same 1–45 Hz 4 s epochs, median-aggregated over epochs and fed into the main logistic model. Time-domain/Hjorth is the one family the brief lists that hasn't been tried, and Hjorth parameters are among the most commonly used features in schizophrenia EEG classifiers. Mobility measures the signal's mean frequency and complexity measures how spread out its frequencies are, as a whole-spectrum shape that the fixed-band relative powers only describe coarsely. Both are ratios of derivative variances, so they don't change with amplitude scale or gain, and the median over epochs keeps them stable on the 1-minute external recordings.

I'm adding graph-theory topology features computed from the wPLI matrices the model already builds. For each band (delta, theta, alpha, beta) I add the log weighted clustering coefficient of the max-normalized graph and the log global efficiency of the mean-normalized graph, giving 8 compact features per condition in the main logistic model. Schizophrenia is repeatedly reported to have less segregated, less small-world functional networks (Micheloyannis 2006; Rubinov 2009), and the current per-channel node strength cannot see that. Both measures are taken on normalized graphs, so they describe network shape rather than overall coupling strength, and wPLI itself does not depend on amplitude scale or reference.
